back.text: King of the gods and god of the sky, thunder, and justice. His thunderbolt and eagle are key symbols; he is brother to Poseidon and Hades.
Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage and queenship. She is Zeus's wife and sister, often shown with a peacock or crown.
God of the sea, earthquakes, and horses. Brother of Zeus and Hades, he wields a trident and is famously quick-tempered.
Goddess of agriculture, grain, and harvest. Her grief when Hades takes Persephone causes the earth to become barren.
Goddess of wisdom, strategy, and skilled crafts; patron of Athens. She is linked with the owl, olive tree, helmet, spear, and aegis.
She sprang fully grown and armed from Zeus's head after he swallowed her pregnant mother, Metis. The story links Athena with Zeus's mind and wisdom.
God of prophecy, music, healing, archery, and plague. Son of Zeus and Leto and twin of Artemis; his symbols include the lyre and laurel.
Goddess of the hunt, wilderness, and childbirth, often associated with the moon. Twin sister of Apollo, she carries a bow and is accompanied by deer.
Goddess of love, beauty, and desire. She is associated with doves, roses, and the sea; differing traditions call her sea-born or a daughter of Zeus.
God of the violent, chaotic side of war. Son of Zeus and Hera, he is associated with weapons, the spear, and the boar and is Aphrodite's lover.
God of fire, metalworking, and craftsmanship. The divine smith makes marvelous objects for the gods; hammer, anvil, and forge identify him.
Messenger of the gods and god of travelers, trade, thieves, and clever speech. Winged sandals and the caduceus identify him; he also guides souls to the Underworld.
God of wine, theater, ecstasy, and transformation. Grapevines, a drinking cup, and ivy are common symbols; his followers include satyrs and maenads.
Goddess of the hearth, home, and household. Her sacred fire represented family and civic unity; she appears in fewer adventures than other Olympians.
Ruler of the Underworld and god of the dead and underground wealth. Brother of Zeus and Poseidon; his helm makes its wearer invisible. He is not the god of evil.
Daughter of Demeter and queen of the Underworld after Hades takes her. Her yearly return to her mother is tied to the renewal of crops.
An older generation of divine beings, children of Gaia and Uranus. Cronus led them before Zeus and the younger gods defeated them in the Titanomachy.
Titan ruler and father of Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hades, Demeter, and Hestia. Fearing overthrow, he swallowed his children until Zeus forced him to release them.
Titan mother of the first Olympian generation and wife of Cronus. She saves the infant Zeus by giving Cronus a wrapped stone to swallow instead.
Gaia is the primordial Earth and Uranus the Sky. Their children include the Titans, Cyclopes, and Hundred-Handers, placing them near the beginning of Greek creation stories.
A Titan and champion of humanity who steals fire from the gods for mortals. Zeus punishes him by binding him while an eagle repeatedly eats his regenerating liver.
God or personification of desire and attraction, commonly shown with a bow and arrows. In later accounts he is Aphrodite's son; in earlier poetry he can be a primordial force.

front.text: Who are the Moirai, or Fates?

back.text: Three goddesses who govern life's thread: Clotho spins it, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos cuts it. Even gods generally respect their decrees.
Nine goddesses who inspire poetry, music, history, dance, and other arts and learning. Poets traditionally invoke them for help telling a story.
Winged goddess and personification of victory. She often appears beside Athena or Zeus, carrying a wreath or palm branch to honor a victor.
Goddess of retribution who restores balance when people become excessively proud or fortunate. She especially punishes hubris—arrogance that challenges proper limits.
Rustic god of shepherds, wild places, and flocks, shown with goat legs and horns. His sudden frightening cries give us the word panic; the panpipes are his instrument.
The greatest Greek strongman, son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene. To atone for a tragedy caused by Hera's madness, he completes twelve seemingly impossible labours.
Hero who kills Medusa by viewing her reflection in a polished shield. He later rescues Andromeda from a sea monster and becomes an ancestor of Heracles.
Hero and legendary king of Athens who enters the Cretan Labyrinth and kills the Minotaur. Ariadne gives him the thread that lets him find the way out.
The greatest Greek warrior in the Trojan War and central hero of the Iliad. His rage after a quarrel with Agamemnon and grief for Patroclus drive the poem.

front.text: Was Achilles invulnerable except at his heel?
front.markdown: Was Achilles invulnerable except at his **heel**?

back.text: That is a famous later tradition: his mother dipped him in the Styx while holding his heel. Homer's Iliad does not include this story, though Achilles is still destined to die young.
Clever king of Ithaca and hero of the Odyssey. His cunning helps the Greeks win at Troy, but pride and divine anger make his voyage home last ten years.
Leader of the Argonauts, who sail aboard the Argo to retrieve the Golden Fleece. He succeeds largely through the magic and help of Medea.
Musician and poet whose singing can charm people, animals, and even stones. He enters the Underworld to recover his wife Eurydice but loses her by looking back too soon.
Daedalus is a master inventor who builds the Labyrinth; Icarus is his son. Escaping Crete on wax-and-feather wings, Icarus flies too near the sun and falls.
A king granted the power to turn whatever he touches into gold. He soon realizes the gift is a curse when food and loved ones can also be transformed.

A daughter of Zeus, famed as the most beautiful woman in the world and wife of Menelaus. Her departure for Troy with Paris becomes the immediate cause of the Trojan War; accounts differ on coercion and choice.
Odysseus's intelligent and steadfast wife, who delays unwanted suitors by weaving a shroud by day and undoing it at night. She tests Odysseus before accepting his identity.
Cretan princess who helps Theseus escape the Labyrinth by giving him a thread to mark his route. He later abandons her; in the best-known continuation she becomes the wife of Dionysus.
Trojan princess given true prophecy by Apollo but cursed never to be believed after rejecting him. She foresees Troy's fall and the danger of the Trojan Horse.
Powerful sorceress and princess of Colchis who helps Jason win the Golden Fleece and escapes with him. When Jason later abandons her, their story ends in devastating revenge.
King of Thebes who unknowingly fulfills a prophecy that he will kill his father and marry his mother despite efforts to avoid it. His search for the truth brings recognition and ruin.
Achilles' closest companion in the Iliad. Wearing Achilles' armor, he drives the Trojans back but is killed by Hector; his death brings Achilles back into battle.
The mortal Gorgon, a snake-haired being whose gaze turns people to stone. Perseus kills her using a reflective shield; Pegasus springs from her body.
Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa, terrifying sisters often shown with snakes for hair. Stheno and Euryale are immortal; Medusa alone can be killed.
A creature with a man's body and bull's head, born to Queen Pasiphaë and confined in the Labyrinth on Crete. Theseus kills it with Ariadne's help.
A many-headed water serpent whose severed heads grow back, sometimes doubled. Heracles defeats it by having Iolaus cauterize each neck; its central head is immortal.
The many-headed hound guarding the Underworld's entrance, preventing the dead from leaving. He is usually shown with three heads and is captured alive in Heracles' final labour.
One-eyed giants. In Hesiod, divine smiths forge Zeus's thunderbolt; in the Odyssey, Polyphemus belongs to a separate race of uncivilized shepherd Cyclopes.
Dangerous singers whose irresistible song lures sailors to ruin. Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast so he can listen safely.
Winged female spirits associated with storm winds and snatching things away. In the Argonaut story they torment the prophet Phineus by stealing or fouling his food.
A fire-breathing hybrid usually combining lion, goat, and snake. The hero Bellerophon kills it while riding Pegasus.

front.text: What is the Sphinx in Greek mythology?
front.markdown: What is the **Sphinx** in Greek mythology?

back.text: A winged creature with a woman's head and lion's body that terrorizes Thebes by posing a riddle. Oedipus answers 'a human,' causing the Sphinx's defeat.
Sea dangers on opposite sides of a narrow strait: Scylla is a multi-headed monster and Charybdis a deadly whirlpool. Odysseus must steer between them.
A divine winged horse born from Medusa when Perseus beheads her. Bellerophon tames Pegasus with Athena's help and rides him against the Chimera.
Beings with a human upper body and a horse's body, often portrayed as wild and unruly. Chiron is the major exception: a wise teacher of heroes including Achilles.

front.text: What happens in the myth of Pandora?
front.markdown: What happens in the myth of **Pandora**?

back.text: Zeus sends the first woman, Pandora, with a sealed jar. When she opens it, hardships escape into human life; hope remains inside. The familiar 'box' comes from a later mistranslation.
He gives humanity fire—and with it technology and civilization—after Zeus withholds it. Zeus chains Prometheus and sends Pandora as part of humanity's punishment.

front.text: How does the myth of Persephone explain the seasons?
front.markdown: How does **Persephone's myth** explain the seasons?

back.text: Hades takes Persephone to the Underworld, and grieving Demeter stops crops from growing. A settlement allows Persephone to return for part of each year, restoring growth, but pomegranate seeds bind her to return below.

front.text: What goes wrong when Daedalus and Icarus escape Crete?
front.markdown: What goes wrong in **Daedalus and Icarus's escape**?

back.text: Daedalus makes wings from feathers and wax and warns Icarus to avoid flying too high or low. Icarus rises toward the sun, the wax softens, and he falls into the sea.

front.text: Why does Orpheus lose Eurydice a second time?
front.markdown: Why does Orpheus lose **Eurydice** a second time?

back.text: Hades permits Eurydice to follow Orpheus out if he does not look back before both reach the upper world. Near the exit, doubt overcomes him; he turns and she vanishes forever.
The beautiful Narcissus rejects others and becomes captivated by his own reflection in water, not realizing what he sees. Unable to possess the image, he wastes away and becomes a flower.

front.text: Why can Echo only repeat other people's words?

back.text: In Ovid's famous version, Hera punishes the nymph Echo for distracting her with chatter, leaving her able only to repeat the last words she hears. Echo later loves Narcissus without being loved in return.

front.text: Why is Arachne turned into a spider?
front.markdown: Why is **Arachne** turned into a spider?

back.text: Arachne boasts that her weaving surpasses Athena's and challenges the goddess. Her work is flawless but insulting to the gods; after the contest and its aftermath, Athena transforms her into a spider.

front.text: What is the punishment of Sisyphus?

back.text: For deceitfully defying gods and death, Sisyphus must push a boulder uphill forever. Each time it nears the summit, the stone rolls back down.

front.text: What is the punishment of Tantalus?

back.text: After gravely offending the gods, Tantalus stands in water beneath fruit he can never reach: the water recedes when he drinks and branches rise when he grasps. His name gives us 'tantalize.'

front.text: How is King Midas freed from the golden touch?
front.markdown: How is Midas freed from the **golden touch**?

back.text: After the gift makes eating and ordinary life impossible, Midas begs Dionysus to undo it. The god tells him to wash in the river Pactolus, which carries the power away.

front.text: Why does King Midas receive donkey ears?

back.text: Midas judges Pan's music better than Apollo's in a contest. Insulted, Apollo gives him donkey ears; the barber who discovers the secret whispers it into the earth, and reeds repeat it.

front.text: What begins the Twelve Labours of Heracles?
front.markdown: What begins the **Twelve Labours of Heracles**?

back.text: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles kills his family in a tragedy. Seeking purification, he serves King Eurystheus, who assigns ten tasks; two are rejected, expanding the total to twelve.

front.text: Which feats make up the first six Labours of Heracles?

back.text: Nemean Lion; Lernaean Hydra; Ceryneian Hind; Erymanthian Boar; Augean Stables; Stymphalian Birds.
back.markdown:
## The first six

1. **Nemean Lion**
2. **Lernaean Hydra**
3. **Ceryneian Hind**
4. **Erymanthian Boar**
5. **Augean Stables**
6. **Stymphalian Birds**

front.text: Which feats make up the final six Labours of Heracles?

back.text: Cretan Bull; Mares of Diomedes; Belt of Hippolyta; Cattle of Geryon; Apples of the Hesperides; capture of Cerberus.
back.markdown:
## The final six

7. **Cretan Bull**
8. **Mares of Diomedes**
9. **Belt of Hippolyta**
10. **Cattle of Geryon**
11. **Apples of the Hesperides**
12. **Cerberus**

front.text: How does Heracles defeat the Nemean Lion?
front.markdown: How does Heracles defeat the **Nemean Lion**?

back.text: Because weapons cannot pierce its hide, Heracles wrestles and strangles the lion. He uses one of its own claws to skin it and wears the hide as nearly invulnerable armor.

front.text: How does Heracles clean the Augean Stables?
front.markdown: How does Heracles clean the **Augean Stables**?

back.text: He reroutes rivers through the filthy cattle yards and completes in one day a task expected to be impossible. Eurystheus rejects the labour because Heracles had arranged payment.

front.text: What is Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece?
front.markdown: What is Jason's quest for the **Golden Fleece**?

back.text: To reclaim his rightful throne, Jason must fetch the Fleece from distant Colchis. He assembles the Argonauts, survives many adventures, and completes King Aeëtes' deadly tests with Medea's help.

Paris of Troy takes Helen, wife of Menelaus, after Aphrodite promises her to him in the Judgment of Paris. Menelaus and allied Greek kings sail to Troy; the deeper mythic causes include divine rivalry and broken oaths.

front.text: What is the main story of the Iliad?

back.text: Not the whole Trojan War, but a short period in its tenth year. Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon, withdraws, returns after Patroclus dies, kills Hector, and finally returns Hector's body to grieving Priam.

front.text: How does the Trojan Horse lead to Troy's fall?
front.markdown: How does the **Trojan Horse** lead to Troy's fall?

back.text: The Greeks pretend to sail away and leave a huge wooden horse as an offering. Trojans bring it inside the city; hidden Greek warriors emerge at night, open the gates, and admit the returned army.

front.text: What is the basic story of the Odyssey?
front.markdown: What is the basic story of the **Odyssey**?

back.text: After Troy, Odysseus spends ten years trying to reach Ithaca while facing monsters, temptations, and Poseidon's anger. At home, Penelope delays suitors; Odysseus returns in disguise, defeats them, and reunites with his family.

front.text: How does Odysseus escape the Cyclops Polyphemus?

back.text: Odysseus calls himself 'Nobody,' gets the Cyclops drunk, blinds him, and escapes beneath sheep. He then boasts his real name, allowing Polyphemus to ask his father Poseidon for revenge.
Greece's highest mountain and the mythic home of Zeus and the Olympian gods. In poetry, their palaces and assemblies occupy a divine realm above ordinary weather.
The realm of the dead ruled by Hades and Persephone. Most souls become shades there; it includes regions of punishment and reward but is not simply equivalent to a later idea of hell.
The most famous river of the Underworld, marking a boundary of the dead. Gods swear binding oaths by it; later tradition makes it the water crossed by Charon's ferry.
A deep abyss below the Underworld, used as a prison and place of punishment. Zeus confines many defeated Titans there; figures such as Sisyphus and Tantalus suffer exemplary punishments.
A blessed afterlife reserved in different traditions for heroes, people favored by the gods, or the virtuous. It is imagined as peaceful and free from ordinary hardship.
Delphi houses Apollo's most famous oracle. The priestess Pythia delivers inspired responses that individuals and cities consult, often in language requiring careful interpretation.

front.text: Why is Crete important in Greek mythology?
front.markdown: Why is **Crete** important in Greek mythology?

back.text: Crete is where Rhea hides the infant Zeus and where King Minos rules. It contains Daedalus's Labyrinth, the Minotaur, and the starting point of Theseus and Ariadne's escape.

front.text: Why is Ithaca important in the Odyssey?
front.markdown: Why is **Ithaca** important in the Odyssey?

back.text: Ithaca is Odysseus's island kingdom and the home he struggles for ten years to regain. Penelope and Telemachus defend his household there from increasingly aggressive suitors.

front.text: Why is Troy important in Greek mythology?

back.text: Troy is the wealthy fortified city in Anatolia besieged by Greek forces for ten years after Helen's departure with Paris. It is home to Priam, Hector, Paris, and Cassandra.
An intricate structure built by Daedalus at Knossos on Crete to contain the Minotaur. Its confusing passages are so effective that Theseus needs Ariadne's thread to escape.
The golden wool of a divine ram, kept in Colchis and guarded by a dragon. Jason must retrieve it to claim his throne, making it the goal of the Argonauts' expedition.
A powerful protective object associated chiefly with Zeus and Athena, depicted as a shield or goatskin breastplate. Athena's aegis often bears the terrifying head of Medusa.
The divine food and drink of the gods, associated with immortality and unfading vitality. Ancient writers are not always consistent about which is food and which is drink.
A ball of thread Ariadne gives Theseus to unwind as he enters the Labyrinth, allowing him to retrace his path after killing the Minotaur. It now means a clue that guides someone through complexity.
Poseidon's three-pronged spear is the emblem of his power over the sea. With it he can stir storms, cause earthquakes, split rock, and create springs.

front.text: Where does Zeus's thunderbolt come from?

back.text: The Cyclopes forge thunderbolts for Zeus after he frees them during the war against the Titans. The weapon expresses his rule over sky and his authority to punish oath-breakers.
A giant wooden horse used by the Greeks to hide warriors inside Troy. Presented as a sacred offering after a false retreat, it enables the surprise attack that ends the war.
Extreme pride or overconfidence that violates proper human limits, often by challenging or disrespecting the gods. In myth it commonly leads to nemesis: punishment or corrective downfall.

The sacred code of hospitality between host and guest: offer food, shelter, gifts, and respect, while guests behave honorably. Zeus protects this custom; violations drive many myths, especially the Odyssey.

front.text: What is the omphalos at Delphi?

back.text: A sacred stone whose name means 'navel,' marking Delphi as the mythic center of the world. Zeus supposedly found the center by releasing two eagles from opposite ends of the earth.
